title: The Throne of Thorns
subtitle: A Coronation, a Covenant, and the Price of Three Centuries of Blood

setting.name: Vermeil Keep and the Throne City of Coronne
setting.description: Vermeil Keep squats at the summit of Lord's Hill like a gilded fist — ancient beyond its dynasty, walled in pale granite quarried before the Empire had a name, its towers crowned with iron stag-heads that watch the city below through hollow sockets. The Keep has stood for three hundred years as a symbol of Vermeil power and the seat of the blood-covenant that underpins it. Tonight, the symbol is to become something far worse. The great audience halls are hung with crimson banners and lit by ten thousand candles; the servants' passages behind their hidden panels swarm with Conclave agents in confessor white; and in the deepest gallery, past the iron-banded doors that no steward living has been permitted to open, the carnelian throne sits cold and ready on its dais of black glass, waiting for the blood that will wake what sleeps beneath it. The city of Coronne is in the grip of the Coronation — the rite has drawn every power in the Empire to the hill, which means that every entrance to the Keep, every rooftop and sewer grate and servants' corridor, is simultaneously the most dangerous and most crucial terrain the party has ever had to cross.
setting.atmosphere: The finale of a long political siege: the beauty of the occasion is a lie the party can see through, and that gap between gilded surface and bloody truth is where they will live and fight. The audience halls smell of beeswax and altar-smoke; the servants' passages stink of damp and fear; and the throne room, when the party finally forces their way in, smells of copper and old stone and something older still — iron and salt and the copper-bright edge of something vast and awake pressing against the thin membrane of the mortal world. The tone is epic and oppressive in equal measure. The clock runs visibly: the Rite of Renewal has a liturgical structure, and the party can hear it progressing through the walls, the resonance of a hundred Conclave voices growing louder and lower with each minute they delay. Every fight they pick in the open risks alerting the Conclave and accelerating the rite. Every fight they avoid costs them time they cannot spare.

keyLocations.name: The Outer Walls and Gatehouse
keyLocations.description: The Keep's outer curtain wall is forty feet of dressed granite pierced by a single main gatehouse on the south approach and two postern doors — one to the servants' quarter (east, near the stables) and one to the old water-cistern (north, long disused). All three are guarded by a combination of the Lord-Regent's household troops in black and gold, and white-robed Conclave wardens whose presence at a military posting would, in ordinary times, be deeply irregular. The rooftops of the gatehouse offer a view of the inner ward, and the cistern postern connects directly to a network of stone drains that opens within the Keep's undercroft.
features: Main gatehouse: portcullis (iron, Strength DC 22 to lift manually, winch inside guardroom), drawbridge over a dry moat twelve feet deep
East postern: guarded by 2 household soldiers and 1 Conclave warden, locked with a heavy padlock (Thieves' Tools DC 17)
North cistern postern: unguarded but submerged to the ankle, rusted door (Athletics DC 14 to force quietly), connects to undercroft drains
Allied approach: if the party has Valmont's forces or Severine's loyalists, a coordinated distraction at the main gate can thin the postern guard to zero for roughly five minutes
Watch patrols on the curtain wall: 2-person patrol, circuits every 12 minutes, overlapping at the northeast tower
encounters: 4 household guards at the main gate (use Veteran stats, CR 3 each)
2 Conclave wardens at each postern (use Cult Fanatic stats, CR 2 each)
If alarm is raised: 8 additional household guards emerge from the inner ward barracks within 2 rounds
secrets: The cistern drain network was mapped by Maddox Quill the Elder during his years as a court entertainer — if he is with the party, he can guide them through without a check
The east postern key is carried by the Keep's head steward, who is currently in the kitchens preparing the coronation supper and can be persuaded or relieved of it without violence
Carmine Veil agents — if the party earned that alliance — have already bribed one gate guard to look the other way at the east postern for exactly one minute beginning at the third bell of evening

keyLocations.name: The Gilded Audience Halls
keyLocations.description: Three connected halls of state occupy the Keep's first floor: the Hall of Petitions, the Grand Receiving Room, and the Banqueting Gallery. Tonight they are packed with minor nobles, church dignitaries, foreign attachés, and two hundred guests who have been invited to witness the 'historic coronation' — most of them have no idea what the Crimson Conclave intends to perform beneath their feet. The halls are ablaze with light and noise, which is both cover and complication: the party can move through the crowds in stolen or genuine court dress, but the Conclave has agents moving through the same crowd, and at least three people in that room know exactly what the party looks like.
features: Hall of Petitions: the first hall, packed with minor gentry and church officials; easiest to infiltrate — the crowd is large, identities unchecked

Grand Receiving Room: where Lord-Regent Crane receives formal congratulations, flanked by Conclave wardens and his personal guard; the hidden panel behind the tapestry of the crimson stag opens to the servants' passages

Banqueting Gallery: where the social elite gather, including anyone who met the party in the Gilded Reach — Lady Vesper Aurelle is here, knows the party on sight, and her allegiance in this moment depends on their relationship
A royal box above the Receiving Room where Puppet Claimant Edren Marsh (see NPCs) waits in ceremonial robes, nervous and pale, flanked by Conclave guards
A side corridor connecting the Banqueting Gallery to the servants' stair, guarded by 1 household soldier who is bored and susceptible to a bribe
encounters: Social navigation: the party must reach the hidden panel without triggering an alarm or alerting the Conclave agents circulating in the crowd
Conclave recognition: 2 Conclave agents (use Spy stats, CR 1) are circulating with descriptions of the party; they will attempt to quietly signal the wardens before confronting anyone
If the party's cover is blown in the halls: 4 household guards and 3 Conclave wardens respond within 1 round; the crowd panics, which provides cover but also chaos
secrets: Lord-Regent Crane is not in the halls — he descended to the throne room an hour ago; his absence should alarm any party member who notices it

Lady Vesper Aurelle, if the party gained her trust in scenario 2, has already smuggled Severine's loyalists into the Keep disguised as kitchen staff; she can point the party to the correct hidden panel

The Puppet Claimant, Edren Marsh, is genuinely terrified and would surrender his claim immediately if privately confronted; he was told this would be a peaceful ceremony and has only just begun to understand otherwise

keyLocations.name: The Servants' Passages
keyLocations.description: Behind every wall of Vermeil Keep runs a second Keep — a labyrinth of plastered corridors, stone staircases, dumbwaiter shafts, and listening alcoves originally built for discretion and now repurposed by the Crimson Conclave as their private highway through the palace. These passages are lit only by hooded lanterns hung at long intervals, the walls sweating with the damp of centuries, and the sound-conducting properties of the old plaster mean that conversation carries around corners in unnerving ways. The Conclave is moving personnel and materials through these corridors right now: parties of robed confessors carrying iron casks, white-gloved functionaries with sealed orders, and at least two Conclave inquisitors in full ceremonial plate who serve as mobile kill-teams if the rite is interrupted.
features: A network of intersecting corridors behind the first-floor halls, the second-floor private apartments, the chapel, and the throne room antechamber
Dumbwaiter shaft connecting the kitchens to the second-floor apartments: large enough for a Small creature or a Medium creature to squeeze through (Athletics DC 15)
Listening alcoves behind the Receiving Room and the chapel: arrow-slit vents covered by sliding panels, usable for eavesdropping without a check if positioned correctly
A collapsed section near the old armory: blocked by fallen stone, requires either an alternate route (adds 5 minutes) or a DC 17 Athletics check to clear quietly

The passage junction beneath the chapel: this is where the Conclave's supply line converges; two iron casks of consecrated blood are staged here, guarded, and are integral to the Rite of Renewal — destroying or tainting them interrupts the rite and buys the party critical time
encounters: Roving confessor pairs (use Cult Fanatic stats, CR 2): 1d4 pairs circulate the passages on irregular schedules; a failed Stealth check draws the nearest pair
Two Conclave inquisitors (use Knight stats with Spellcasting: can cast Hold Person DC 15 as a bonus action, 3/day) stationed at the passage junction beneath the chapel
If the casks are attacked: the inquisitors immediately signal the throne room; Mordent Vale will know within 1 round
secrets: Brother Caelum Voss, if he survived and is with the party, knows these passages from his time as a reform confessor assigned to the Keep; he can navigate them without checks and knows which panels open to which rooms

The sealed orders carried by one functionary contain Mordent Vale's contingency plan: if the rite is interrupted, Crane is to be sacrificed to the Carnelian directly, buying enough blood to partially incarnate the entity even without the formal rite

A cache of Conclave correspondence hidden inside a false panel near the chapel contains written evidence of the Emperor's poisoning — signed by Crane, countersigned by Vale — which could be devastating in the right hands after the crisis is resolved

keyLocations.name: The Keep Chapel and Antechamber
keyLocations.description: The Keep's private chapel occupies a high-ceilinged room adjacent to the throne room, separated from it by a pair of iron-bound oak doors twelve feet tall. The chapel has been transformed for tonight into a staging area for the Rite of Renewal: the pews have been pushed back, the floor chalked with the covenant sigils, the altar draped in crimson rather than the Communion's usual white. A dozen lesser confessors maintain a continuous low chant here that feeds, through the open inner doors, into the main rite in the throne room. The antechamber between the chapel and the throne room proper is the final chokepoint before the endgame: it is guarded by the Conclave's elite Scarlet Wardens, and it is where the party will face their last fight before reaching Mordent Vale.
features: The chapel: the chanting confessors (12 lesser confessors, use Cultist stats CR 1/8) are not fighters — they break and flee if combat erupts, but their presence in the rite means the chant falters and the rite is slowed by one stage

The covenant sigils chalked on the floor: a character proficient in Religion or Arcana can attempt to corrupt the sigils (DC 18 Arcana, takes 1 full action per sigil, 6 total), each corrupted sigil further slows the rite and inflicts 2d6 psychic damage on the Carnelian when the final confrontation begins
Iron-bound inner doors to the antechamber: barred from the antechamber side; can be forced (Athletics DC 20) or unlocked if the party has the chapel master's iron key

The antechamber: a stone room twenty feet square, the air thick with incense and the hum of the rite resonating through the walls; murder holes in the ceiling (Conclave archers above, active only if the alarm has been raised)
encounters: The Scarlet Wardens: 4 Conclave elite guards (use Berserker stats with +2 AC from plate, CR 4 each) in crimson-lacquered armor, stationed two in the chapel and two in the antechamber
If the murder holes are active: 3 Conclave archers (use Thug stats with longbows) in the ceiling crawlspace; removing the ceiling grate requires DC 14 Athletics
secrets: One of the Scarlet Wardens, a woman named Hallin, was recruited by force — her family is being held as surety for her loyalty; if confronted with this fact (Insight DC 14 to notice her distress, Persuasion DC 16 to reach her), she will stand aside and unlock the inner doors
The chapel master's key is hanging on a hook behind the altar, partially concealed by the crimson drape, visible on a DC 12 Perception check

keyLocations.name: The Throne Room and the Vault Beneath
keyLocations.description: The oldest room in Vermeil Keep is a long gallery of black basalt and pale marble, lit by iron torchères whose flames burn unnaturally steady in air that tastes of iron. At the gallery's far end, raised on three steps of polished black glass, sits the Crimson Throne — the carnelian seat, larger than it appears in paintings, its surface veined with something that is not quite stone and never quite still. In the stone beneath the throne, directly below the dais, a vault door of ancient iron stands open tonight for the first time in living memory, and from the darkness below it rises a warmth and a resonance that is not sound but pressure, the sense of something enormous pressing against the inside of its prison. Lord-Regent Crane stands at the throne's left hand in formal chancellery robes, pale and sweating. High Confessor Mordent Vale stands before the throne in full Conclave regalia — a mask of hammered carnelian over his upper face, a stole embroidered with the covenant sigils in crimson thread — conducting the Rite of Renewal in a voice that has not wavered in three hours. Around the gallery's perimeter, a ring of twenty Conclave confessors maintain the blood-wards: standing in pools of consecrated blood drawn in channels across the floor, their linked arms forming a ritual circle that keeps the growing presence of the Carnelian contained within the chamber. The Puppet Claimant waits at the foot of the throne steps, trembling, awaiting the moment Vale bids him be seated.
features: The Crimson Throne: the carnelian seat is both a piece of furniture and a conduit; any creature that sits in it while the blood-covenant is active must succeed on a DC 20 Charisma saving throw or be overwhelmed by the Carnelian's will for 1 minute; on a success, the creature may speak one command that the covenant enforces on all bound parties for 1 hour

The blood-ward channels: the channels of consecrated blood carved into the floor feed the rite and contain the Carnelian's influence; disrupting a channel (Athletics DC 12 to smash, or any fire damage) breaks the ward at that point, but breaking all six channels simultaneously causes the Carnelian to lash out in all directions before the party can control it

The open vault: a stairway descends twenty feet into a chamber of ancient worked stone where the covenant was first sealed; the Carnelian's presence is overwhelming here (DC 15 Wisdom save at the top of each round or suffer the Frightened condition until end of turn); the covenant stone is here — a slab of carnelian inscribed with the original blood-oath — and destroying it (AC 15, 60 HP, resistance to all damage except radiant and force) breaks the covenant permanently

The iron torchères: their flames respond to the Carnelian's emotions — they flare blood-red when the entity is enraged, gutter near-black when it is feeding; a character who watches them can track the rite's progress
The gallery pillars: eight stone pillars down the length of the room provide three-quarters cover to Medium creatures; the perimeter confessors are each stationed between two pillars
encounters: Mordent Vale: high-CR cult leader caster — see Combat Encounters in Act 3 Scene 2 for full description
The Carnelian avatar: a partially-incarnated blood-entity — see Combat Encounters in Act 3 Scene 2 for full description

Perimeter confessors (20 Cultists, CR 1/8 each): not fighters, but they maintain the blood-ward; incapacitating or killing a confessor breaks one blood-ward segment; if eight or more are incapacitated, the ward collapses and the Carnelian is no longer contained within the room (this is catastrophic — the entity's influence floods the upper Keep)

Lord-Regent Crane: uses Noble stats (CR 1/8); he attempts to flee down the vault stairs when combat begins; if caught and confronted with the evidence from the servants' passages, he collapses into abject capitulation — he is not brave, only ambitious
secrets: The Carnelian is not fully incarnated yet; it needs the Puppet Claimant to be seated in the throne with his blood shed across the carnelian surface; stopping the seating stops the final stage of incarnation

Nyssa Vael, if she is a party member, will feel a terrible pull toward the vault stairs — her patron is the Carnelian, and the entity recognizes her blood; she must make a DC 18 Wisdom saving throw when she first enters the throne room or move toward the vault for 1 round involuntarily; on a success she resists but understands in that moment the full truth of her heritage

Magister Elias Crane, if present, recognizes his distant cousin the Lord-Regent in the room and must succeed on a DC 12 Wisdom save or use his reaction to call out to him rather than acting in the first round; on a success he steels himself and can act normally

synopsis: The campaign reaches its bloody terminus. The succession crisis that began with a body in an alley and a dead man's ledger has drawn the party from the gutters of the Shamble to the gates of Vermeil Keep itself, and now the gates must be forced. High Confessor Mordent Vale has set the Rite of Renewal for Coronation Night — the single evening when every faction in Coronne is gathered and distracted, when the blood-covenant's liturgical calendar aligns, when the puppet Lord-Regent Crane is positioned to be crowned and then to shed the blood that will wake the Carnelian fully and forever. The party arrives at the Keep with whatever they have built: alliances earned through three scenarios of dangerous choices, allies who may or may not still stand beside them, a knowledge of the covenant's true nature that no one outside the Conclave is meant to possess, and a choice they must make before the night is over. They can storm the gates, slip through the servants' passages, or call in every favor they have ever earned to force the audience halls — but however they enter, the path leads to the throne room, to Mordent Vale, and to the Carnelian entity rising through its prison of stone. The climax is not a single battle but a gauntlet: infiltrate the Keep, disrupt the rite, survive the final confrontation, and then — in the silence after the last blow is struck — decide what happens to the Crimson Throne and the covenant that gives it power.
hook: The party knows. They know who murdered the Emperor, they know what the Conclave intends, and they know that tonight is the last night it can be stopped. The Rite of Renewal is tied to the covenant calendar — if it is not performed at this coronation, the Carnelian will wait another century, and Mordent Vale and Crane will have the throne in the meantime, which may be worse. Word reaches the party in whatever safe house or rallying point they have used through the campaign: the gates of Vermeil Keep opened at sunset. The coronation procession enters at the third bell of evening. The rite begins at midnight. They have hours. Whatever allies they have cultivated — Princess Severine's loyalists with the palace seal, Duke Valmont's advance riders who slipped into Coronne ahead of his marching army, Carmine Veil agents with access to half the locks in the city, Captain Holt's Watch officers who were never comfortable with what the Conclave was doing — are waiting for word. The party has to decide how hard to hit the gate, how quietly to move, and what they intend to do when they reach the throne. All they know for certain is that if they are wrong about any of it, the next coronation will be performed by a god.

acts.title: Act 1: The Gates of the Gilded Prison
acts.description: The party breaches Vermeil Keep. Whether they force the gates, slip through the servants' passages, bluff their way in through the audience halls, or execute a coordinated assault with allied forces, this act is about getting inside and getting oriented before the rite advances beyond the point of no return. The Keep is not a dungeon — it is a living political space on the most consequential night of its history, full of people who are not enemies, some of whom can become unexpected allies if approached correctly. The party must choose how loudly to announce themselves, because the choice echoes through everything that follows.
objectives: Breach Vermeil Keep by whatever means the party's alliances and skills allow
Make contact with any allied forces staged inside or outside the Keep
Locate the hidden entrance to the servants' passages
Establish the rite's current stage and how much time remains
Avoid triggering a general alarm that would lock down the throne room before the party is in position

scenes.name: A Night for Coronations
scenes.description: The party approaches Vermeil Keep in the hour before the third bell. The city of Coronne is arrayed for celebration and unease in equal measure: colored lanterns hang across the high city streets, crowds press against the cordons on Lord's Hill road, and the Sanguine Cathedral across the river is dark, its bells silent — the Communion's resources have relocated to the Keep tonight. The party must assess their approach, coordinate with any allies, and make the opening move.
scenes.readAloud: "Lord's Hill is lit from summit to base like a torch left burning on an altar. The road that winds up from the Gilded Reach is lined with lanterns of crimson and gold, and the crowd that has gathered to watch the coronation procession three hours ago has not entirely dispersed — men and women in their best clothes pressed against the guard-rope barriers, speaking in low, uncertain voices. They expected pageantry. What they feel, even out here in the open air, is something else: a pressure in the teeth, a copper taste at the back of the throat. The great gates of Vermeil Keep stand open at the summit, pouring light into the dark like a wound. Through them you can hear the distant sound of the coronation — strings and voice and beneath it, just barely, something that is not music. The bell in the Lord's Hill clock tower reads a quarter-hour to the third bell. You have, by your best reckoning, two and a half hours before Mordent Vale reaches the final stage of the rite. The Keep's outer walls are close enough now to see the silhouettes of sentries on the curtain. Somewhere in that gilded box, an empire's fate is being decided without you. That is about to change."

skillChecks.success: You spot the guard rotation on the curtain wall — two soldiers, circuiting northeast every twelve minutes. The east postern is guarded by three figures: two in the black and gold of the household, one in confessor white. The north cistern door is unguarded and barely visible in the shadows at the base of the wall.
skillChecks.failure: The wall sentries are present but you cannot determine their rotation from this distance. You will need to get closer before the approach.

skillChecks.success: The crowd's unease is not purely the ambient anxiety of a succession crisis. Several people in the gathering have the fixed, distant look of people who sense something is wrong and cannot name it. The pressure in the air is the Carnelian's influence bleeding through the walls — it has been awake for hours, feeding on the blood-ward rite, and it is already touching the world outside.
skillChecks.failure: The crowd seems anxious but crowds always are at moments of political change. Nothing in particular stands out.

skillChecks.success: Examining the gatehouse from a distance, you notice that the Conclave wardens on the curtain wall are carrying carnelian tokens — small polished chips of red stone worn at the throat. These tokens are keyed to the blood-ward inside; a character carrying one of these tokens will not be attacked by the ward's aura effects. Acquiring one would be valuable.
skillChecks.failure: The gatehouse appears to be standard military fortification with no obvious weaknesses visible at this distance.

enemies: 4 Veterans (CR 3 each) at the main gate
2 Cult Fanatics (CR 2 each) at the east postern
combatEncounters.tactics: The Veterans fight in pairs, one engaging while the other calls for reinforcements; they are professionals who are not afraid of the party, only of Vale's Conclave handlers who outrank them. The Cult Fanatics at the east postern will not retreat — they have been told that anyone attempting to enter without authorization is an enemy of the covenant and must be stopped at any cost. If the party has Valmont's soldiers or Severine's loyalists creating a distraction at the main gate, the postern guards are distracted for one full minute and the Stealth DC to pass them drops to 10.
combatEncounters.terrain: The approach road is wide open, no cover within forty feet of the gatehouse. The postern door alcove is shadowed and cramped — two Medium creatures can fight side by side at most. The cistern door is in a recessed alcove full of dead leaves and old ironwork; fighting there means the cistern pool (knee-deep water, difficult terrain) is immediately inside.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This scene rewards the party's accumulated choices across three scenarios. If they have Severine's loyalists, Lady Vesper Aurelle has already moved people inside as kitchen staff and can pass a message via the crowd. If they have Valmont's riders, three dismounted soldiers in civilian dress are waiting at a specific doorway near the servant entrance and will create a diversionary brawl near the main gate on signal. Carmine Veil agents, if bought, have compromised the east postern bribe for exactly one minute at the third bell. Captain Holt, if the party cultivated the Watch, has pulled his patrol from the north approach 'due to a staffing dispute' — leaving the cistern door effectively unguarded. Play the alliance payoffs as smooth and satisfying. Play the absence of an alliance as a meaningful complication. The party earned or didn't earn this entry, and the scene should feel like it.
loot: 2 carnelian ward-tokens taken from Conclave wardens (grant immunity to the blood-ward's passive aura effects inside the throne room)
East postern key (from the head steward if persuaded, or taken from a defeated Cult Fanatic)
A household guard's black and gold tabard (useful as disguise for a Medium humanoid)
A confessor's white stole taken from a defeated warden (grants cursory passage among lesser Conclave personnel — DC 13 Deception to maintain)

scenes.name: Behind the Tapestry
scenes.description: Inside the Keep, the party must navigate the gilded audience halls or slip directly into the servants' passages. Either way, they are now in the belly of the beast — surrounded by people, some of whom want them dead, some of whom are terrified, and at least one of whom is desperate for rescue. The clock is audible: somewhere beneath the floor, muffled by stone and ceremony, the Rite of Renewal has begun its second hour.
scenes.readAloud: "The gilded halls of Vermeil Keep are everything the Shamble is not, and tonight they are wrong in all the ways that beauty can be wrong. Candles by the thousands. Crimson and gold everywhere, on the banners, on the tablecloths, on the formal dress of two hundred guests who are laughing a little too loudly and drinking a little too fast, the way people do when they sense that something beneath the occasion is not right but cannot afford to say so. Through the floor — you feel it more than hear it — a resonance that is not quite sound moves in slow pulses, like a heartbeat learning to be a heartbeat again. The hidden panel is behind the tapestry of the crimson stag on the east wall of the Grand Receiving Room. Between you and it: forty feet of crowded floor, two Conclave agents moving through the press with the patient attention of men who are looking for someone, and the brilliant, dangerous gaze of Lady Vesper Aurelle, who has just seen you from across the room and whose expression, you note with some relief, is not alarm. It is something closer to grim satisfaction."

skillChecks.success: You move through the crowd without catching the attention of the Conclave agents. Lady Vesper Aurelle falls into step beside you as if by coincidence, angling you smoothly toward the east wall without appearing to do so. She murmurs: 'Your Severine people are in the kitchens. The Crane man is already below. You have less than two hours. The panel releases with three raps, middle height.'
skillChecks.failure: One of the Conclave agents pauses, studies your face, and begins moving in your direction. You have one round to act before he is within speaking distance.

skillChecks.success: You notice that the Puppet Claimant, Edren Marsh, is visible in the royal box above — and he is not watching the ceremony below with the calm of a man about to be crowned. He is gripping the rail with white knuckles, his eyes moving from exit to exit. He looks like a man who has just understood what kind of celebration this is.
skillChecks.failure: The royal box is visible but its occupant's expression is unreadable from this distance and angle.

skillChecks.success: If the party speaks with Edren Marsh (requiring either reaching the royal box or sending a written note via a bribed servant, DC 11 Sleight of Hand), he immediately and frantically agrees to cooperate. He will withdraw from the ceremony, refuse to be seated at the throne, and provide testimony against Crane if the party can guarantee his safety. He is not brave but he is genuinely horrified by what he has stumbled into.
skillChecks.failure: Edren Marsh cannot be easily reached or is too frightened to respond coherently to written contact. He remains in the royal box, a problem to be solved later.

enemies: 2 Spies (CR 1 each) in the crowd acting as Conclave agents
4 Veterans (CR 3 each) if the alarm is raised in the halls
combatEncounters.tactics: The Conclave agents prefer to signal the wardens rather than fight in public — they are not combatants, and a brawl in the audience halls would be as bad for the Conclave as it would be for the party. If confronted quietly, they will try to detain the party and call for help. If exposed publicly and shown to be agents of the Conclave, a Persuasion DC 17 check turns the crowd's anxiety into active resistance against them, buying the party two rounds of chaos to use as cover. The Veterans respond to any raised alarm in military fashion — they push through the crowd from the hall entrances in a cordon.
combatEncounters.terrain: The Grand Receiving Room is forty by sixty feet, packed with guests (crowd counts as difficult terrain, grants half cover). The east wall tapestry is forty feet from the main entrance. The hidden panel requires standing still for one action to operate it.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This scene is the social fulcrum of the scenario. The party is surrounded by non-combatants who are not enemies, and the instinct to draw weapons should be resisted in favor of social maneuvering. Lady Vesper Aurelle's assistance (if earned) should feel like a graceful gift — she is good at this in ways the party never will be, and watching her redirect two Conclave agents with a smile and a misunderstanding should be a pleasure. The Puppet Claimant is a loose thread that becomes either an asset or a complication depending on whether the party reaches him. If Rowan Ashdown or Maddox Quill is in the party, they are in their element here and should be given moments to shine.
loot: A sealed letter from Lady Vesper Aurelle, addressed to her legal counsel, that constitutes a public withdrawal of her family's support for Lord-Regent Crane's claim (political value, no gold value)
Edren Marsh's formal signet ring (if he cooperates), usable to seal documents as a claimant's authorization
A Conclave agent's coded dispatch, partially decoded: references to 'the contingency' and 'the Crane alternative'

acts.title: Act 2: Through the Hidden Passages
acts.description: The party enters the servants' passages and fights their way toward the throne room through the Keep's hidden arteries. This act is about stealth, disruption, and the escalating sense that the rite is running ahead of them. The party can slow the rite by destroying the blood-cask supply line, corrupting the covenant sigils in the chapel, and taking out Conclave personnel — each disruption buys time and weakens the Carnelian's emergence. But every disruption also risks alerting Mordent Vale, who may accelerate the rite's critical stages if he knows the party is inside.
objectives: Navigate the servants' passages to the chapel without triggering a general alarm
Disrupt the Conclave's ritual supply line at the passage junction beneath the chapel
Deal with the Conclave inquisitors guarding the junction
Enter the chapel and corrupt as many covenant sigils as possible before the Scarlet Wardens respond
Force the iron-bound inner doors to the antechamber

scenes.name: The Hidden Veins of the Keep
scenes.description: Behind the panel in the Grand Receiving Room, the party enters the servants' passage network. The difference from the gilded halls is immediate and absolute: bare plaster, pooled shadow, the smell of tallow and stone damp, and the low throb of the rite vibrating through the walls. The passages are not empty. The Conclave is moving supply and personnel through them, and the party must thread a needle between engagement and speed.
scenes.readAloud: "The panel swings inward on counterweights worn smooth by centuries of use, and the air that comes through is cold and smells of wet stone and something sweeter and worse beneath it — the copper warmth of the consecrated blood moving through the passages in its iron casks. The servants' corridor is lit by a single hooded lantern at the far end, its light a dim orange that turns the plastered walls the color of old skin. The sound is different here. The music from the halls above is gone. What replaces it is a resonance in the stone itself, a slow pulse that you feel in the fillings of your back teeth and the bones of your forearms. It is patient. It is hungry. It is growing. Somewhere ahead, closer than you want, you hear the shuffle of leather soles on stone, and the faint clink of iron against iron — the casks. You have perhaps thirty seconds before whatever is carrying them rounds the corner."

skillChecks.success: You press flat against the passage wall and let the pair of robed confessors pass without seeing you. As they round the corner ahead, you catch a glimpse of the iron cask between them — sealed with lead and stamped with the covenant sigil. The cask leaks faintly at one seam, leaving a dark bead on the floor.
skillChecks.failure: The confessors freeze and turn. They have not yet cried out — they are not certain what they have seen. You have one round to act before they decide.

skillChecks.success: Reading the layout of the passages from the junction marks scratched into the plaster at each intersection (a navigational system for servants who memorized the code), you map the route to the chapel junction without needing to backtrack. The junction beneath the chapel is two right turns and a descending stair.
skillChecks.failure: The passage markings are opaque without the servant code. Navigation requires either a guide or trial and error — there is a one-in-three chance of taking a wrong turn at each intersection, each costing three minutes.

skillChecks.success: The resonance in the walls is not ambient — it is directional. The Carnelian's hunger pulls toward the throne room like a compass, and by attending to its pressure you can navigate the passages by feel, always moving against the pull to travel away from the throne room, always following it to move toward. You need no map.
skillChecks.failure: The resonance is disorienting rather than informative. It makes concentration difficult and adds a vague sense of being watched.

enemies: 2 Cult Fanatics (CR 2 each) carrying iron casks
2 Knights with Hold Person (CR 3 each) at the chapel junction
combatEncounters.tactics: The Cult Fanatics will not drop the casks to fight — they are fanatically committed to delivering them. This means they fight at disadvantage (one hand occupied) unless cornered, at which point they set the casks down and become fully dangerous. The Knights at the junction are the Conclave inquisitors — veteran fighters enhanced by blood-rite consecration that gives them +2 to attack rolls while within thirty feet of the casks. They open with Hold Person targeting the most dangerous-looking party member and close to sword range on anyone not paralyzed. Destroying the casks (AC 12, 8 HP each, the contents splash outward and are ruined) eliminates the Knights' consecration bonus but stains a ten-foot radius with blood that is difficult terrain.
combatEncounters.terrain: The passage corridor is eight feet wide, the junction chamber twelve feet square. Low ceiling (seven feet) prevents flying or jumping over opponents. The casks can be used as improvised shields (half cover) or weapons (1d6 bludgeoning, then they crack and spill). The descending stair to the chapel is ten feet wide and has no railing — a shoved character must succeed on DC 13 Dexterity save or fall prone at the base of the stair.

scenes.roleplayNotes: Brother Caelum Voss is invaluable in this scene if the party has kept him close — he knows the passages and can guide them without checks. Give him a moment of quiet resolve here: he has spent his life inside the Sanguine Communion and is now walking through its hidden corruption in the Keep that his church has controlled. The weight of that should show. The iron casks are a moral as well as tactical choice: destroying them is obviously tactically useful but the party may feel the cost of what is in them. The blood inside was donated by Communicants who believed in the rite. This is not the Conclave's evil alone — it is the Empire's.
loot: 2 iron casks of consecrated blood (if not destroyed: ritual components worth 200 gp to a church scholar, or can be used to disrupt the rite by other means if brought intact into the throne room)
A Conclave inquisitor's carnelian ward-token (as found at the outer wall)
A set of Conclave confessor robes taken from the defeated Cult Fanatics (disguise set, appropriate for a Medium humanoid)

scenes.name: The Chapel of Sigils
scenes.description: The party reaches the Keep's private chapel and faces the Conclave's ritual infrastructure at its most tangible: the covenant sigils chalked on the floor, the chanting confessors who feed them, and the Scarlet Wardens who guard the iron-bound doors to the throne room antechamber. This is the last staged position before the endgame, and how the party handles it determines how hard the final confrontation will be.
scenes.readAloud: "The chapel doors are not locked from the passage side — there is no expectation that anyone should reach them from within the walls. They swing open onto a room that was once a place of quiet prayer and is now something between a ritual circle and a staging area. The pews have been pushed to the walls. The floor is covered in chalk symbols — the covenant sigils — each two feet across, arranged in a precise geometric pattern that covers the entire nave from altar to narthex. A dozen robed confessors stand at intervals around the perimeter, eyes closed, lips moving in a continuous low chant that you can feel rather than hear, a syllabic pressure that makes the chalked lines vibrate faintly with each repetition. The altar at the far end has been redressed in crimson. On it, a single iron bowl catches a slow drip from a cracked cask above it, the blood falling in metronomic drops that keep time with the chant. And flanking the great iron-bound doors at the nave's far end, standing like statues in their crimson-lacquered plate, are the Scarlet Wardens. Four of them. They have been waiting for this. One of them — a woman, her visor up, her expression the flat blank of someone who is deeply unhappy with her orders — meets your eyes for a moment. Then looks away."

skillChecks.success: You identify the structure of the sigil array and understand which symbols are load-bearing in the ritual sequence. There are six primary sigils; corrupting them in order (moving clockwise from the altar) maximizes the effect. Each corrupted sigil will deal 2d6 psychic damage to the Carnelian when the final confrontation begins and slows the rite's progression by an additional increment.
skillChecks.failure: The sigils are clearly ritual in nature but their specific function and optimal disruption sequence are opaque to you. You can still try to corrupt them but do so without the tactical advantage of understanding which are most important.

skillChecks.success: The unhappy Scarlet Warden is not performing theater — her distress is genuine. A character who approaches her quietly (requiring the other Wardens to be occupied or the party to separate her from her colleagues) and names what they know about her situation has a real chance of reaching her. She is Hallin, and she would rather be anywhere else.
skillChecks.failure: The Warden's brief eye contact is impossible to read. She has resumed her formal stance and her face gives nothing away.

skillChecks.success: The confessors' chant is a liturgical piece called the Covenant Renewal — you have heard fragments of it in the Communion's public rites, but these are the inner verses, the ones the public never hears. The chant itself is not evil, but it is being used as a key to unlock something the original composers never intended. Disrupting the chant by any means — even something as simple as a Silence spell or a sudden loud noise — breaks the resonance and forces the rite back one stage.
skillChecks.failure: The chant is recognizable as Communion liturgy but you cannot determine its specific function in the ritual context.

enemies: 4 Scarlet Wardens (use Berserker stats, AC 18 in plate, CR 4 each)
12 Chanting Confessors (Cultist stats, CR 1/8 each — non-combatants who flee if combat erupts)
combatEncounters.tactics: The Scarlet Wardens fight with two-handed weapons and are trained to fight in pairs — one engages while the other watches the flanks. They do not pursue beyond the chapel; their orders are to hold the doors, not to chase intruders through the passages. Warden Hallin can be separated from the group with a DC 16 Persuasion check (or automatically if the party named her situation beforehand); if she stands down, the fight is three-on-party instead of four, and she will unlock the iron doors when combat is resolved. The chanting confessors break and scatter the moment a weapon is drawn — they are not fighters, and their flight actually disrupts the chant, buying the party one rite-stage of time at no additional cost. The Wardens will not pursue the confessors. They have their orders.
combatEncounters.terrain: The chapel nave is thirty by sixty feet. Sigil array on the floor is difficult to move through quickly without smudging it (DC 12 Dexterity at the start of each turn while moving through a sigil square, or the sigil is accidentally corrupted — this has the same effect as intentional corruption but counts as rushed and produces only 1d6 psychic damage instead of 2d6). The iron bowl on the altar is fragile (AC 10, 5 HP); destroying it stops the blood-feeding and breaks one blood-ward segment in the throne room above.

scenes.roleplayNotes: The covenant sigils are the party's best non-combat contribution to weakening the Carnelian before the final fight. Every action spent corrupting a sigil is an action not spent in combat, so the party has to decide how much time they can spend here versus how much they need to move. The confessors' flight is a gift — use it to show that ordinary people caught up in the Conclave's machinery are not the enemy, and that the Conclave's power depends on compliance that is not actually unconditional. Warden Hallin's potential defection is the emotional payoff for a party that has learned to look for the person behind the uniform. If they reach her and she stands aside, let the moment breathe. She has chosen badly for a long time. This is her one good choice.
loot: A Scarlet Warden's carnelian ward-token (each warden carries one)
The Warden Hallin's master key to the Keep's restricted areas (if she cooperates), including the inner doors and the vault stairs
A sealed Communion liturgical scroll: the full text of the Covenant Renewal chant, annotated in Vale's own hand — evidence of the Conclave's inner workings, legally and theologically devastating
The iron bowl from the altar (if recovered intact): still holds consecrated blood, can be used in the final confrontation to disrupt one blood-ward segment at range

acts.title: Act 3: The Blood and the Throne
acts.description: The party forces the antechamber and enters the throne room. Everything has converged here: all the alliances, all the evidence, all the choices made across four scenarios. High Confessor Mordent Vale has been conducting the Rite of Renewal for three hours and is near the final stage — the blood-seating of the Puppet Claimant that would complete the Carnelian's incarnation. The fight is not merely a combat but a race against the rite, and the party's disruptions in Act 2 determine how much time they have. At the end of the fight, whatever survives of the party must make the defining choice: who sits the throne, and what becomes of the covenant.
objectives: Clear the antechamber of its guards
Enter the throne room and interrupt the Rite of Renewal before the Puppet Claimant is seated
Defeat or neutralize High Confessor Mordent Vale
Defeat or banish the Carnelian avatar if it partially incarnates
Make the final choice: who rules Veldoran, and what becomes of the blood-covenant

scenes.name: The Antechamber of Last Things
scenes.description: The iron-bound doors to the antechamber open onto the final approach to the throne room — a stone room twenty feet square, thick with incense smoke and the humming resonance of the rite at near-completion. Whatever guards remain here must be dealt with quickly; every round spent here is a round Mordent Vale spends on the rite's final stage.
scenes.readAloud: "The antechamber is not large — a stone room barely twenty feet across, its walls bare of ornament save for iron sconces burning with low orange flames. The incense here is so thick you taste it on your teeth, a sweet resinous smoke that catches in the throat and makes the eyes water. Beyond the far door — tall, arched, slightly ajar — you hear Mordent Vale's voice clearly for the first time. It is not what you expected. It is quiet. Not a preacher's voice, not the commanding roar of a zealot at the height of triumph — a quiet voice, patient as stone, reading words in the old Veldoran dialect with the unhurried precision of a man who has been practicing this moment for thirty years. He is not performing. He is working. The antechamber is not empty. Two armored figures stand before the far door with the particular stillness of people whose entire attention is on the space behind it — facing away from you, because no one was supposed to come this far. You have, perhaps, one surprise. Use it well."

skillChecks.success: You cross the antechamber without the guards hearing you over the resonance of the rite. The surprise round is yours.
skillChecks.failure: One of the guards turns at the last moment. Surprise is lost, but you are still in the room and the distance is short.

skillChecks.success: Through the gap in the far door, you can see into the throne room. Mordent Vale stands before the throne, his back to you. The Puppet Claimant has been brought down from the royal box and stands at the foot of the throne steps, held gently at each elbow by Conclave wardens. Lord-Regent Crane is pressed against the far wall, as far from the vault as the room allows, looking at the open vault stairs with the expression of a man who has been told what is in the water and cannot stop thinking about whether the bridge will hold. The ring of perimeter confessors is intact. You have, by your estimate, two exchanges of the rite's call-and-response before Vale reaches the seating stage.
skillChecks.failure: The room beyond is partially visible but the angle and the incense haze prevent a clear reading of what stage the rite has reached.

enemies: 2 Conclave inquisitor-knights (use Knight stats, +2 attack bonus from blood-rite consecration, CR 3 each)
combatEncounters.tactics: These guards are veteran fighters who respond instantly to any sound. If surprised, they must use their first action to turn and draw weapons (if sheathed) rather than attack. Otherwise, they form up side by side to block the far door, using their shields to screen each other. They call out to the throne room immediately upon engaging — unless a Silence spell is active in the antechamber or a party member uses a reaction to physically cover one of their mouths. If Warden Hallin's key was used to open the inner doors silently, the guards are not yet alert and surprise is much easier.
combatEncounters.terrain: The antechamber is twenty feet square with no cover — nowhere to hide, nowhere to retreat. The far door is ten feet wide. A character who charges through the far door mid-combat while the guards are occupied brings the fight into the throne room, which alerts Vale immediately but may be preferable to spending more rounds in the antechamber.

scenes.roleplayNotes: The antechamber is deliberately small and spare — this is not a boss room but a transitional space, and it should feel like one. The party is one door away from the end of three scenarios of work, and that tension should be played up rather than down. Vale's quiet voice through the door is more frightening than any shout could be. If the party has a character who can make out the words of the rite's current stage (Religion DC 13), give them a specific line: 'Let the heir of the covenant be brought forward, that the bargain may be renewed in his blood.' That is the sentence before the seating. They have very little time.
loot: 2 carnelian ward-tokens from the defeated inquisitors
A set of antechamber keys carried by one inquisitor (redundant with Hallin's key but confirms the party now has full access to every lock they have encountered)

scenes.name: The Rite of Ruin
scenes.description: The throne room. The final confrontation. The party bursts through the far door into the long basalt gallery, and everything the campaign has built to — all the factions, all the secrets, all the blood — comes due in this room, in this hour. High Confessor Mordent Vale will not surrender. The Carnelian will not wait. And when the last blow falls, the party will stand in a room with an empty throne and a broken covenant and the whole of Veldoran waiting for someone to tell it what happens next.
scenes.readAloud: "The throne room door opens onto the longest room you have ever stood in, and the first thing you understand is that the air here is not right. It breathes. Not the ventilation of a large space — it breathes, slowly, with purpose, as though the room itself is an organism and you have just entered its chest cavity. The carnelian throne at the far end glows. Not brightly — a deep internal warmth, like a coal two breaths from igniting, pulsing at intervals that match nothing except, after a moment, the rhythm of your own blood. The chalked covenant sigils on the floor — or what remains of them, accounting for any your party corrupted in the chapel — pulse with it. The ring of white-robed confessors holds the perimeter, their linked arms forming the blood-ward circle, their faces blank with the particular emptiness of people who have handed their will to someone else. Lord-Regent Crane is against the far wall to your right, looking at the open vault stairs with shining eyes. The Puppet Claimant is at the foot of the dais, shaking, held gently by wardens who seem not to notice. And before the throne, facing you at last, stands Mordent Vale. He is smaller than you imagined. The carnelian mask covers his upper face; below it, a mouth that is not smiling, not surprised, not afraid. He studies you for one full second. Then: 'You are very capable,' he says quietly, 'for people who have made such a fundamental error. The rite is already complete enough. Even if you stop the seating, what wakes beneath this stone will not return to sleep merely because the ceremony is interrupted. The Carnelian does not need a covenant. It needs blood. And you have brought quite a lot of it into this room.' Beneath the vault stairs, something shifts. The warmth in the throne deepens. And from the open vault, climbing with the patient confidence of a thing that has not moved in three centuries and finds it finds it finds it finds it is not difficult, something begins to emerge."

skillChecks.success: You recognize the precise stage of the rite and understand that Vale is right in one sense and wrong in another: the Carnelian can partially incarnate on the spilled blood in this room regardless of whether the formal rite concludes, but without the covenant renewal, the incarnation is unstable. The entity must feed continuously or it will be forced back. If the party can survive the combat without losing any characters to death — without the blood-debt being paid — the Carnelian's emergence will collapse under its own instability within ten minutes. It cannot be allowed to kill anyone in this room.
skillChecks.failure: Vale's claim about the rite's completion is impossible to evaluate in the chaos of the moment. You will have to trust the outcome.

skillChecks.success: Lord-Regent Crane is not a fighter and his nerve is broken. A direct appeal — showing him the signed confession found in the servants' passage, or confronting him with the evidence from the ledger, or simply telling him clearly that Mordent Vale has already written his death into the contingency plan — causes him to break entirely. He orders his household troops to stand down, destroying the military threat outside the throne room (if any remains) and depriving Vale of his political backing in one move. He will not help fight. He sits against the wall and covers his face. But he is no longer a weapon in Vale's hand.
skillChecks.failure: Crane is too far gone in fear and complicity to respond to reason in the moment. He remains pressed against the wall, neither helping nor hindering, until the fight resolves.

skillChecks.success: A character can attempt to drag the Puppet Claimant away from the warden escorts (Athletics DC 15 against the wardens' contested Strength) or disrupt a blood-ward segment by overturning a consecrated channel in the floor (Arcana DC 15 to identify the correct segment, Athletics to physically break it). Either action changes the tactical landscape of the fight.
skillChecks.failure: The wardens hold the Claimant firmly, or the blood-ward channel is too deeply carved in the stone to disrupt without tools.

enemies: High Confessor Mordent Vale (custom high-CR villain, see tactics)
The Carnelian Avatar (custom CR 9-11 entity, see tactics)
2 Conclave Warden pairs (4 Cult Fanatics, CR 2 each) holding the Puppet Claimant and guarding the vault stairs
combatEncounters.tactics: HIGH CONFESSOR MORDENT VALE: Vale is a CR 9 antagonist built on the Priest stat block with significant upgrades. He uses the following abilities. Spellcasting (Wisdom-based, spell save DC 17, +9 to hit): Cantrips — Toll the Dead, Sacred Flame, Guidance. 1st — Inflict Wounds, Shield of Faith, Bane, Command. 2nd — Spiritual Weapon (appears as a carnelian shard), Hold Person, Silence. 3rd — Bestow Curse, Dispel Magic, Animate Dead (uses this to raise any character who drops to 0 HP as a temporary servant of the Carnelian — this is his cruelest ability and should be the one the party fears most). 4th — Banishment, Death Ward (cast on himself at the beginning of combat as a precast). 5th — Contagion, Flame Strike (flavored as erupting blood). He has 130 hit points and AC 17 from his consecrated ceremonial plate beneath his robes. Vale's tactics: in the first round, he casts Silence centered on himself (removing the party's verbal spells and his own, which he accepts — he intends to fight hand-to-hand with his ceremonial mace enhanced by Spiritual Weapon, while the Carnelian handles the magic). Second round, he moves to engage the most physically dangerous party member personally, using his Spiritual Weapon to threaten a second target. If a party member drops to 0 HP, he uses his reaction to cast Animate Dead — this should be horrifying and personal. If reduced below 40 HP, he begins moving toward the open vault stairs; reaching them and descending is his escape and his last gambit (the Carnelian's power is strongest at the vault floor and would restore him partially). Vale will not surrender. He has spent thirty years preparing this night and he genuinely believes in the covenant's necessity. He is not afraid of death; he is afraid of failure. Play him as cold, precise, and utterly committed. THE CARNELIAN AVATAR: The entity emerges from the vault over the first three rounds of combat — round 1, a tide of red-black liquid rises to floor level; round 2, limbs of crystallized blood and carnelian shard form at the vault's lip; round 3, the avatar pulls itself fully into the throne room. It is approximately CR 10 in effective challenge. Appearance: a twelve-foot figure of semi-liquid carnelian and crystallized blood, its outline shifting, vaguely humanoid but wrong in proportion, with too many limbs and a face that is a series of concentric apertures like a flower opening. It does not speak. It radiates hunger as a physical sensation. Statistics in narrative form: AC 16 (natural armor of crystallized blood, shatters and reforms), 160 HP. Damage Immunities: poison, psychic. Damage Resistances: fire, cold, bludgeoning and piercing from nonmagical weapons. Damage Vulnerabilities: radiant, force. Speed 30 ft, does not need to breathe. Actions: Bloodlash — melee attack, +9 to hit, reach 10 ft, 3d8+5 bludgeoning damage plus 2d6 necrotic damage; on a hit the target must succeed DC 16 Constitution save or their maximum HP is reduced by the necrotic damage dealt (restored on a long rest). Crimson Spray — recharge 5-6 — 30-foot cone, DC 16 Dexterity save, 4d8 necrotic on fail, half on success; creatures that fail are coated in consecrated blood and have disadvantage on saves against the Carnelian's Legendary Resistance until the blood is washed off. Legendary Actions (3 per round, taken at end of other creatures' turns): 1 action — Beckon (one creature within 60 ft must succeed DC 15 Wisdom save or use their movement to move toward the Carnelian, no action required); 2 actions — Drain (one creature within 10 ft takes 2d10 necrotic damage, Carnelian regains HP equal to half the damage dealt); 3 actions — Sanguine Surge (the Carnelian makes one Bloodlash attack as a legendary action). Lair Effect: at the start of each of the Carnelian's turns, each creature in the throne room must succeed on a DC 13 Wisdom saving throw or be Frightened of the Carnelian until the start of their next turn. Characters carrying a carnelian ward-token have advantage on this save. The avatar retreats to the vault if reduced below 40 HP unless the covenant stone in the vault has been destroyed; if the stone is destroyed first, the avatar takes 20 force damage and is Stunned for 1 round.
combatEncounters.terrain: The throne room gallery is eighty feet long and thirty feet wide. The basalt pillars (eight total) provide three-quarters cover to Medium creatures. The blood-ward channels (if not disrupted in the chapel) are carved channels in the floor that function as difficult terrain when the Carnelian avatar is active — the blood in them flows toward the entity and any creature that steps in a channel takes 1d4 necrotic damage. The open vault stairway at the far end of the room behind the dais is a 5-foot-wide descending stair — the Carnelian cannot fit on the stairway (too large for the opening) but can reach into it with one arm. The dais steps are three shallow risers of black glass that are difficult terrain to ascend in combat conditions. The Crimson Throne: any creature that sits in the throne during combat must succeed on DC 20 Charisma save or be dominated by the Carnelian for 1 minute; on a success, the creature can issue one binding command to the covenant. If the covenant stone in the vault is destroyed while a creature occupies the throne, that creature takes 6d10 force damage (Charisma save DC 18 for half) as the covenant shatters through them.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This is the most complex scene the party has faced, and it should feel earned. Vale's Animate Dead ability is the nightmare option — the thought of fighting a fallen companion is viscerally awful, and even the threat of it changes how the party manages their resources. Make sure it is used at least once if the opportunity presents (a party member drops to 0 HP). The Carnelian avatar's emergence should be staged theatrically across three rounds, giving the party time to process what they are looking at before they have to fight it. The confessors on the perimeter are not fighters — if the party or an ally calls on them directly and personally to stop (Persuasion DC 15, or automatically if their chant has already been disrupted in the chapel), several of them will break the circle and flee, which collapses portions of the blood-ward and weakens the avatar. Lord-Regent Crane's fate should be left to the party. He is not dangerous. He is pitiable. Whatever they do with him — arrest him, shame him publicly, give him a controlled opportunity to recant — is appropriate, and the option to simply let him sit against the wall while history happens around him is also available. The Puppet Claimant Edren Marsh is another choice: the party can get him out of the room safely (he will cooperate with anyone who takes charge), use him to disrupt the rite (his refusal to approach the throne, stated clearly, breaks the rite's final stage without violence), or — grimly — the DM can note that Vale has a contingency for this: he will attempt to force the seating with Crane's blood if Edren Marsh is removed, which is mechanically the same outcome but politically devastating for Crane. The fight's conclusion should be allowed to breathe. When Vale falls and the Carnelian avatar is driven back or destroyed, there is a moment of silence before the choice. Honor that silence.
loot: Mordent Vale's carnelian mask (a masterwork item of hammered carnelian worth 800 gp as an art object, or can be destroyed to sever the Conclave's symbolic authority — the two options are mutually exclusive)

Mordent Vale's consecrated ceremonial mace (a +2 mace, requires Attunement; while attuned, the wielder can cast Toll the Dead as a cantrip; the mace hums faintly with covenant resonance and may have further significance if the party retains it through a rebroken covenant)

The covenant stone fragments (if the stone in the vault was destroyed): inert shards of carnelian, no magical properties, but of immense historical value — physical proof of the blood-covenant's existence and destruction
Crane's signed confession (if recovered from the servants' passage cache): a complete record of the Emperor's assassination, signed by Crane and countersigned by Vale

The contents of the vault antechamber: three centuries of accumulated tribute to the Carnelian — 1,200 gp in ancient coin of pre-dynastic minting, a set of six matched carnelian goblets (worth 150 gp each), two scrolls in the first Emperor's hand describing the original terms of the blood-covenant (priceless as historical documents), and a +1 shortsword of ancient make with a carnelian pommel-stone (Blood-Debt Blade: deals an additional 1d6 necrotic damage against any creature that has drawn blood from the wielder in the last 24 hours)

npcsInvolved.name: High Confessor Mordent Vale
npcsInvolved.description: A man of late middle years, lean and precise in his movements, with close-cropped grey hair and the kind of stillness that comes from decades of absolute conviction. The carnelian mask he wears in formal rites is not theater — it is the outward sign of an inward devotion that has consumed every other aspect of his identity. He was once a genuine reformer within the Sanguine Communion, a young confessor who believed that the covenant could be steered toward justice rather than exploitation. When he first descended into the Sanguinarium and understood what the covenant actually was, he did not recoil. He leaned in. He has spent thirty years preparing the Rite of Renewal, not because he is power-hungry — he wants nothing for himself — but because he genuinely believes that the Carnelian's full incarnation is the next stage of the covenant's evolution, the moment when the transaction becomes mutual rather than merely extractive. He is wrong, catastrophically and sincerely wrong, and he is completely beyond the reach of argument.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Vale believes the Carnelian's incarnation will create a living covenant — a permanent bond between the Empire and its patron entity that will end the fraying instability of the past decades. He sees the Emperor's murder not as assassination but as mercy, removing an unsuitable vessel to clear the way for the renewal. He does not expect to survive the night and does not particularly want to — his role ends when the rite is complete. He is not afraid of the party; he is disappointed in the waste of capable people.

npcsInvolved.name: Princess Severine Vermeil
npcsInvolved.description: The late Emperor's only acknowledged child is twenty years old tonight and moving through the city with more guards than she has ever been allowed to command, the palace seal in her pocket, and a face that has learned in three scenarios to reveal nothing it does not choose to reveal. She is not in the Keep at the start of this scenario — she is in a safehouse in the Gilded Reach, coordinating her loyalists through Lady Vesper Aurelle, waiting for the signal from the party. If the party sends for her, she arrives within twenty minutes, which means she can be present for the choice at the end of the fight but not for the fight itself. She is frightened and does not show it, and she is far more grateful than she knows how to say.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Severine wants the throne because she believes she can heal the Empire — and increasingly, because she understands what the alternative is. She is not a warrior; she is a politician, and the thing she offers is the legitimate succession that prevents civil war with Valmont's forces. If the party crowns her, she will not forget that she is alive because strangers from the Shamble decided she was worth saving. She will also never, for the rest of her reign, be entirely comfortable in the throne room, which she considers appropriate.

npcsInvolved.name: Duke Roderick Valmont
npcsInvolved.description: Valmont is not inside the Keep tonight — his legion is two days' march from Coronne, and his advance riders who slipped into the city are his intelligence assets and his message-carriers, not his fighting force. He is connected to events in the throne room only through the party's choices. If the party sends word to Valmont that the Conclave has been exposed and Crane is discredited, Valmont sends a formal declaration to the city gates pledging to stand down his march in exchange for recognition of his legitimate grievance against House Vermeil. This opens the possibility of crowning him by proxy — the party can use Edren Marsh's signet or Crane's capitulation to legitimize Valmont's claim — but Valmont himself will not arrive until after midnight, which may be too late to matter.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Valmont wants recognition, justice, and a throne that governs rather than exploits. He does not want a civil war. He is not a monster; he is a proud man with a legitimate grievance who has been pushed to a dangerous position by the Conclave's manipulation. If the party gives him a path to legitimacy that does not require war, he takes it. If they give him the throne, he is a harder ruler than Severine but a more stable one, and the military crisis ends overnight.

npcsInvolved.name: Lord-Regent Aldous Crane
npcsInvolved.description: The chancellor who has served three emperors is fifty-three years old tonight and looking every year of it. He went into the Conclave's arrangement believing it was a political alliance — he would provide legitimacy and administrative control, they would provide backing and remove obstacles, and together they would manage a stable transition. He did not fully understand the Rite of Renewal until six weeks ago. He has been unable to find a way out since then, and the understanding that Vale's contingency plan involves his own blood has crystallized a fear that was already close to panic. He is in the throne room because he has nowhere else to be and no courage left to run.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Crane wants, at this point, only to survive. He will capitulate completely to anyone who offers him a credible path out of this room. He is guilty of conspiring in the Emperor's murder and will confess to it in writing if he believes confession is the price of his life. He has no loyalty to Vale; the Conclave was always a tool that has now turned in his hand. If arrested rather than killed, he is a political weapon — his testimony against the Conclave is devastating, and his capitulation removes the last legitimate fig leaf from the Conclave's political position.

npcsInvolved.name: The Puppet Claimant — Edren Marsh
npcsInvolved.description: Edren Marsh is twenty-four years old and distantly descended from a legitimizing cadet branch of House Vermeil on his mother's side — distant enough that his claim requires a great deal of legal architecture to stand, but the Conclave's legal team has been building that architecture for two years. He was recruited eight months ago under the impression that he would be a ceremonial figurehead. He was told three weeks ago what the Rite of Renewal actually entails and has been under effective house arrest since then. He is not evil. He is not brave. He has done nothing wrong except be born with the right grandmother and have the kind of ambitious hunger that makes a man say yes to flattering offers without reading them carefully. He is wearing ceremonial robes that are too large for him and shaking visibly.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Edren wants out of this room. He will cooperate with the party unconditionally and immediately. He is not a claimant in any meaningful sense — he is a prop, and he knows it. If the party secures his safety, he will provide written renunciation of his claim and testimony against the Conclave's legal framework.

npcsInvolved.name: Wren 'Sparrow' Quill
npcsInvolved.description: If the party has maintained their relationship with Wren through the campaign, she is outside the Keep tonight with a small team of Veil operatives, running interference on the city-side of the crisis — managing informants, intercepting Conclave communications, and keeping the Watch's neutral units from being turned against the party by anyone with coin and authority. She is not a fighter at this level of play and will not enter the Keep, but she can be reached by message and can provide intelligence, safe passage out of the city afterward, and the Mother of Knives' neutrality as a political gift.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Wren has been in over her head since the night she refused to recover Corvin Ashe's ledger. She has committed to seeing this through, which is the kind of commitment that either ends careers or defines them. If the party wins, she has a debt called in by the most interesting people in the city. She considers this adequate compensation.

npcsInvolved.name: Captain Holt of the City Watch
npcsInvolved.description: Captain Holt pulled his patrol from the north approach because the paperwork required for a Watch unit to enter the Keep grounds during a coronation is genuinely complex and he has chosen to interpret his orders very literally tonight. He is not brave enough to openly back the party and not corrupt enough to actively oppose them. If the party wins and emerges from the Keep with a credible claim to have stopped a Conclave conspiracy, Holt will be the first Watch officer to offer his cooperation. He is a fair-weather ally with enough institutional knowledge to be useful in the aftermath.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Holt is a realist. He has been a realist his entire career, which is why he is still alive and still captain. The Conclave has been making him uncomfortable for months, and the Watch's neutralization in the poorer districts has been eating at him in ways he has not allowed himself to articulate. If the party hands him a version of events he can report upward with a straight face, he will report it exactly that way.

npcsInvolved.name: The Carnelian
npcsInvolved.description: The entity bound in the carnelian throne for three hundred years does not have human motivations. It has hunger and it has patience and it has the accumulated weight of three centuries of slow feeding, and it has been awake and aware for far longer than Mordent Vale realized. It did not engineer the succession crisis — it simply recognized the conditions that would create an opportunity and allowed the Conclave to believe they were acting on their own initiative. It is not evil in a conventional sense; it is old and it is hungry and the covenant is the only thing that has ever limited it. If the covenant is broken, the Carnelian is not freed — it is simply no longer bound, which is worse. If the covenant is renewed cleanly without incarnation, the entity retreats, diminished, to its prison. If it is destroyed in the vault, the throne is merely a chair.
npcsInvolved.motivation: The Carnelian wants to be fully in the world. It does not want to rule; it wants to feed. It has no interest in Veldoran's politics, only in its blood. Every dynasty, every church, every generation of Communicants has been food. The blood-covenant was never a gift — it was a leash, and the leash is fraying.

rewards.gold: 1,200 gp in ancient coin from the vault, plus 150 gp per carnelian goblet (6 total, 900 gp), plus the monetary value of sundry items taken from defeated enemies — approximately 2,500 gp total accessible in this scenario
items: Mordent Vale's Ceremonial Mace (+2 mace; while attuned, wielder may cast Toll the Dead as a cantrip; hums with residual covenant resonance)
Blood-Debt Blade (shortsword +1; deals additional 1d6 necrotic damage against any creature that has dealt damage to the wielder in the last 24 hours)
Six Carnelian Goblets (masterwork art objects, 150 gp each, or politically charged as gifts to noble houses)

The First Emperor's Covenant Scrolls (priceless historical documents; two scrolls in pre-dynastic Veldoran script describing the original terms of the blood-covenant and the Carnelian's nature — potentially the most important documents in the Empire's three-hundred-year history)

Mordent Vale's Carnelian Mask (800 gp as an art object if preserved; if destroyed in the throne room, its destruction is witnessed by any surviving Conclave members and serves as the symbolic dissolution of their authority)
Crane's Signed Confession (a legal document, no gold value; priceless as a political instrument to legitimize whatever regime the party supports)
Edren Marsh's Renunciation (a written legal renunciation of his claim, signed and sealed — removes the Conclave's puppet claimant from the succession legally)
rewards.story: The story outcome of this scenario is entirely the party's choice, and the DM should present each as a genuine possibility with real costs and real gifts. ENDING 1 — CROWN SEVERINE: Princess Severine Vermeil is crowned in the throne room with the covenant broken (or the stone merely cracked, allowing a clean renewal without incarnation). She is the legitimate heir, the civil war with Valmont is averted through diplomatic negotiation (Valmont accepts a formal recognition of his grievance and a promise of military reform), and the Empire enters a period of fragile but genuine recovery. Veldoran still has all its old problems — the granaries, the corruption, the hollow institutions — but it has a monarch who knows where the bodies are buried and why they need to stay there. The party becomes, quietly, the most important people in Coronne. Severine never forgets. ENDING 2 — BACK VALMONT: The party uses Crane's capitulation and Edren Marsh's renunciation to clear the succession field and sends word to Valmont's advance riders that the throne is his if he marches peacefully. Valmont enters Coronne at dawn, takes the throne, and is crowned without ceremony. He is a harder ruler than Severine — less polished, more direct, with a soldier's contempt for court procedure — but the military crisis ends immediately, the granaries are reopened by order, and the Conclave's political power is broken by royal decree within a fortnight. The party is rewarded generously and finds they have traded a clever friend for a blunt one. ENDING 3 — THE THRONE DESTROYED: The party descends into the vault and destroys the covenant stone, shattering the blood-covenant entirely and rendering the carnelian throne inert. The Carnelian is not destroyed — it is merely unbound and retreats to wherever such things retreat, diminished. The throne is still a chair; whoever sits in it is just a person. The succession crisis is not resolved by this action — it still has to be worked out politically, and the party may need to advocate for a specific outcome. But the dark bargain at the Empire's root is severed. Veldoran will have to learn to govern without the covenant's supernatural backing for the first time. The Empire faces an uncertain future, entirely its own. ENDING 4 — A PARTY MEMBER CLAIMS THE THRONE: Any character who sits in the carnelian throne after the covenant stone is destroyed takes 6d10 force damage (Charisma DC 18 for half) — and survives as the new occupant of a merely significant chair in a merely significant room. They are not empowered by the covenant. They are claiming the throne the hard way, with the social and political weight behind them. If the character has the faction support to make that claim stick (Severine's backing, Valmont's recognition, or the Watch's cooperation), it can work. It is not easy. It is extraordinarily complicated. It is also the kind of outcome that makes the best stories.
