ENDING 5 — THE COVENANT RENEWED CLEANLY: If the party prevents the Carnelian's full incarnation but chooses not to destroy the covenant stone — perhaps because they need the Empire's supernatural stability, perhaps because a character (Nyssa Vael, most obviously) has a relationship with the entity that complicates simple destruction — the covenant can be renewed without the Rite of Renewal's blood-incarnation component. This requires a DC 20 Arcana or Religion check and the willingness of a character to place their hand on the covenant stone and speak the old binding words (found in the First Emperor's scrolls). The character who does this takes 4d10 necrotic damage and forms a personal link to the Carnelian — they will hear it, distantly, for the rest of their life. The covenant persists, diminished and re-bounded. The Empire retains its supernatural stability. The cost is ongoing.

twists: Mordent Vale is not the only one who has been preparing for this night for thirty years. The Mother of Knives — the unseen head of the Carmine Veil — has been positioning her people inside the Keep since before the Emperor died, not to support the Conclave, but to be in position to take the carnelian mask and the covenant scrolls if the rite succeeded. Her agents are in the Keep, observing. If the party defeats Vale and claims the vault, a Carmine Veil agent approaches them quietly afterward with an offer: the Mother of Knives would like to meet. She has been collecting leverage on the covenant for thirty years and she has opinions about what the party should do with the scrolls.

The carnelian throne has been awake longer than the Conclave knows. The Carnelian has been nudging events for decades — the Emperor's deteriorating health, the grain shortages, the Watch's corruption — not to control outcomes but to create instability that would yield blood. Mordent Vale is not a mastermind; he is a very capable instrument. The real architect of the succession crisis is sleeping in the vault.

Nyssa Vael's patron has been the Carnelian all along — not a distant patron communicating through eldritch whispers but the entity bound below the throne, leaking influence through the covenant's fraying edges and finding a bloodline sensitive enough to receive it. When Nyssa enters the throne room, the Carnelian recognizes her. What that means is the DM's choice: it could mean the entity tries to use her, or that it is afraid of her, or that she alone can speak to it in a way that no one else in the room can. Give Nyssa's player a moment that is only hers.

Lord-Regent Crane did not poison the Emperor alone. He was not even the first choice — the original plan called for a Carmine Veil assassination, contracted through the Mother of Knives, who subcontracted it, and the chain of custody has been broken in three places. Crane's confession, when it comes, implicates three noble houses, two church officials, and a name the party may recognize. The conspiracy is wider than even the campaign suggested, and its full unwinding will take the next monarch years.

The Carnelian covenant has a clause the first Emperor wrote and the Conclave never found: a release condition. If the blood-debt is paid in full — a precise sum described in the First Emperor's scrolls — the entity is dissolved, not merely rebound. The sum is significant. It may be exactly the blood already spilled this night, in this room, if the party had allies who fell. This twist is for DMs who want a bittersweet ending: the covenant could have been ended cleanly, and the cost was already paid, if only the party had the scrolls in time to read them.
dmTips: The scenario's central mechanical challenge is the rite's clock. Establish early that the rite progresses in stages and that the party's actions — destroying the blood-casks, corrupting the sigils, disrupting the chant — push the clock back. Keep a simple six-segment tracker visible to yourself: the party's disruptions push it left, time passing pushes it right. If the tracker reaches completion before the party enters the throne room, the Carnelian enters the fight already partially incarnated (gains 40 additional HP and its Lair Effect is active from round one). If the party disrupts all possible elements, the Carnelian must spend its first legendary action of each round on Beckon rather than Drain (it is hungry and reaching rather than feeding and growing). Make the tracker a felt presence rather than a literal prop — count the rite's stages in narrative terms, not numbers.

Alliance accounting is the other central element. Before running this scenario, review the party's relationship with each faction and note which alliance payoffs are earned. Severine's loyalists inside the Keep as kitchen staff, Valmont's distraction at the gate, Veil agents with the postern bribe, Holt pulling his patrol — each is only available if the party cultivated that relationship across scenarios 1-3. Do not award unearned alliances, but do not undervalue earned ones. An alliance payoff should feel like a clean, satisfying click — the work paid off. The party should enter the throne room feeling the weight of everything they built to get there.

Mordent Vale is the emotional core of the villain cast. He is not mad, not stupid, not cruel in a conventional sense — he is genuinely, completely wrong in a way that has consumed him so thoroughly that he cannot see it anymore. Play him as a man who believes he is saving the world, right up to the moment he drops. If any party member attempts to argue with him during the fight (Persuasion or Insight checks), give Vale a real response that reveals his worldview — do not let him be a cardboard apocalyptic. He has a counter-argument for everything. It is the wrong counter-argument, but it is not a stupid one.

The Carnelian avatar's three-round emergence is the most important staging decision in the fight. Round one: the vault door exhales warmth and the torchères flare blood-red. The blood in the floor-channels begins to flow toward the vault. Round two: something reaches up from below, fingers of crystallized carnelian curling over the vault lip, twelve feet of something hauling itself against gravity and three centuries of binding. Round three: it is in the room, and it is looking at everyone at once, and everyone in the room knows immediately and without being told that it is deciding who to feed on first. Do not rush this. The party deserves to see what they came here to stop.

The final choice — who rules, what happens to the covenant — should never feel rushed. When Vale is down and the avatar is dealt with, give the room a breath of silence before anyone speaks. Describe what the throne room looks like: the blood on the floor, the extinguished torchères, the carnelian throne sitting cold and still. Then let the party decide. If they have Princess Severine summoned, she arrives in this silence. If Valmont's rider is in the city, he can be reached. Give the party the full weight of the moment. They have earned it. Whatever they choose, honor it completely — including the endings where things are complicated, or imperfect, or bittersweet. The Crimson Throne is not a story where the good ending is obvious. It is a story about what people choose when they finally have the power to choose.

Nyssa Vael's connection to the Carnelian is the campaign's deepest personal thread and the DM should have decided before this session what it means. The simplest version: when Nyssa enters the throne room and the Carnelian recognizes her, she hears its voice clearly for the first time — not eldritch whispers but something more intimate, something that calls her by the name her grandmother used and offers her the covenant for herself. She can refuse. Give her player the choice privately, on a folded note if possible. Whatever she decides, it should be hers.

The session-end content is as important as the combat. After the throne room is won and the choice is made, the campaign is not over in the narrative sense — the aftermath of three scenarios of political work needs at least a half-session of epilogue. Who is crowned, and what does that coronation look like? What happens to the Conclave's rank and file, the lesser confessors and wardens who were following orders? What does Crane's confession do to the noble houses it implicates? What is the Mother of Knives offering, and does the party accept the meeting? Is there a character epilogue for each PC who survives? The Crimson Throne is a political campaign and political campaigns do not end with the battle — they end with the treaty. Give that treaty the time it deserves.
